videos.title: louise broadfoot   progressing talented athletes and related integrity risks (1080p)

segments.description: Please welcome Louise Broadfoot, senior integrity officer at Tennis Australia, a former professional cricketer and member of Australia's 2005 World Cup winning team. Louise has also served 20 years in the police force and completed a deployment to Afghanistan as an Army Reserve officer. Today she will be presenting progressing talented athletes and related integrity risks, sharing her insights on safeguarding the pathway for young athletes. Let's welcome Louise. In Coach Athlete Dynamics, in our environment, the reason we educate on professional boundaries and grooming is so that we can all help protect our sport together and notify the integrity team of behaviour that doesn't feel right to you. In that regard, it's also important for you to know how to raise issues and we'll cover off on this as well later in the presentation. So grooming is a term that can carry slightly different meanings depending on definitions in criminal law or policies. So for our purposes today, we're referring to conduct where the actions taken by a person have hidden intentions of later forming an inappropriate, intimate or possibly sexual relationship with a person under the age of 18 years of age. So we're now going to discuss the process of grooming in a sport context, how actions that blur professional boundaries can actually be a sign of grooming, but can also simply be poor professional behaviours

and then the impact that this can have on the reputation of the coach, the business and the player. But firstly, we're certainly not suggesting that all coaches are potentially grooming kids for later abuse, but it is important to understand that the small minority of people who do cause harm to children are actually across every profession in our communities, including our own. Today we'll talk about the process that abusers often do take so that you can recognise certain behaviours in others and understand how your own actions, which may be completely innocent, could be misrepresented or perceived. And obviously this process could just as easily apply to a teacher, a family member or any other person in a position of influence over children. So the grooming process is all about eroding barriers and inhibitions, taking advantage of the trust that has been established and the imbalance in power between a coach and a junior player and gradually normalising and escalating offending behaviour. It's not as linear as it may appear here, however these are the main hallmarks of the grooming process. The first step is identifying and targeting a potential victim. This person may be vulnerable due to a difficult family life, parents who are busy, absent or disengaged or from a low socioeconomic background or many other reasons. In a recent Australian example where a tennis coach was convicted

of sexually related criminal offences against a teenage athlete, the victim's survivor was in difficult financial circumstances and the coach offered her a compassionate scholarship to attend his high performance program. In addition, as the judge remarked here, the athlete was particularly vulnerable due to her family situation. Also, the child may be eager to please due to a combination of many factors such as their vulnerability, someone showing them attention or simply that they are desperate to succeed or in other words, coachable. We'll discuss coachability in a bit more detail later. The second step in the grooming process involves developing a trusting, friendly relationship with the child and quite possibly with their adult caregiver. We know that successful coaches really do need to understand the personality of their players to help them achieve success on the court. This means helping players understand their emotions, their reactions, their experiences which assist them in dealing with pressures and maximising their performance. These things all build towards the player trusting their coach completely. It's this high level of trust which can create vulnerability in a person if a person wanted to exploit that. Often it's not just the children who are being groomed, the parents also need to feel comfortable allowing their child to spend a significant amount of time with someone and in a high

performance context, parents want to believe that their child could one day make it and play at the highest level and this may lead to them ignoring certain warning signs in the coach and player relationship. As well as the face-to-face contact such as at training sessions, there is also likely to be an element of online contact or communication. We're just going to show you now some examples of text messages that the Australian coach who was convicted of sexual offences had sent to the player. These messages became more frequent and the content more personal over time. So as you read the messages, consider the age difference. We're talking about someone in their forties compared to the junior player being sixteen and the power imbalance as a result of the coach and player relationship and the scholarship that was held. Now to the third step in the grooming process. Again in a performance context and an individual sport such as tennis, it is easy to isolate a child from their usual friendship networks especially those outside tennis with additional training sessions, trips away and so on. The child might also be emotionally isolated from support networks either by building jealousy or resentment towards others or excessive dependency on the groomer. The groomer may start to emotionally manipulate and control the child such as by making them feel special. We saw some clear examples of this in the

text messages just now. They may also pretend to be vulnerable themselves somehow, start to ask more intimate questions and introduce concepts of secrecy or things only the two of them should know such as inappropriate comments or jokes with sexual innuendo. The groomer has become a central figure in the child's life and they link themselves closely to any chance of future success in tennis for the player. Throughout this process the groomer has been taking incremental steps to assess the child's response and to normalise their inappropriate actions. They are gradually eroding barriers that should normally exist be that in an adult child relationship or a coach athlete relationship. In a sporting context this could easily be disguised as a requirement for the athlete's performance such as assisting the athlete to stretch or giving massages which can then also lead to physical abuse. As an example this was seen to be the situation in the case of Larry Nasser who was the USA Gymnastics Doctor who is now in jail for numerous child sex offences. The athlete A documentary on Netflix about Nasser is actually really worth watching if you don't know about this particular case. The offending behaviour may also include online abuse, sending or requesting intimate images, expressions or love or desire. It might often be framed as joking using a laughing emoji or similar but this may also be fishing to gauge the

child's boundaries and their responses. In some cases it might include introducing illicit behaviour such as drinking alcohol and it's often the case that a child in these situations doesn't know how to respond to an adult due to the power imbalance and they may appear to be willingly participating but truthfully they are really uncomfortable and don't know how to make it stop. There is also almost always a demand for secrecy such as instructing the child to delete massages or photographs or threatening to expose their behaviours to friends or parents. So we recently heard a keynote speech by Mary Kane who's a former world junior champion in 3000m running and was the victim of physical and emotional abuse at the hands of US track and field coach Alberto Salazar as part of the Nike Oregon project athletics program. Salazar has since been banned from coaching and the Nike Oregon project has been disbanded. Mary made some interesting observations about being a coachable athlete and how it played a part in her being vulnerable to abuse. Some traits of coachable athletes are firstly that they show appreciation for a coach's time and feedback by actively listening and learning from them. Coachable athletes don't talk back or become defensive when a coach gives them feedback. A US college sport coaching website says that humble athletes accept that their coach knows best and this is the right mindset for a developing young

athlete. Coachable athletes recognise that in order to achieve their goals they will have to make sacrifices and work hard. Sacrifices often refers to missing out on the life of a normal teenager. And of course as a coach this makes an athlete easier to work with. I mean who wants to have their advice questioned or not taken on board? But this mindset can also create vulnerability in the athlete and lead to an environment in which abusive practices can be allowed to develop. Issues can exist such as a coach promoting the attitude of the coach knows best so don't question anything and that they are the sole source of wisdom and hold the key to future success. The coach also has total control over the training environment and can make examples of athletes who push back or challenge their views or instructions. So this can then be a barrier to junior athletes in raising things that they genuinely aren't feeling comfortable with. Also overly invested parents will listen to and believe the coach to pursue their own dreams and what they believe their child wants. Parents may allow abusive behaviours from a coach thinking that they are necessary and part of the sacrifice in order for their child to succeed at all costs. Athletes and parents place a huge amount of trust in coaches which can isolate the athletes from other peer networks and leave them vulnerable to abuse. As we recognised earlier being a coachable athlete is a really

positive trait that coaches like to see in junior players. However we need to also be aware that this trait creates vulnerability in junior athletes and this vulnerability can be exploited by a person or coach acting with inappropriate or abusive intentions. And we're not trying to dictate how to coach here but what we are saying is consider the environment you are creating and whether you are developing players who are overly compliant which may make them vulnerable to inappropriate behaviour. As coaches we genuinely want players to succeed but there is also a commercial reality that players need to feel the coach is important to their success. Otherwise they might question the value of our coaching service to them. Getting the balance right and maintaining high levels of professionalism is critical. So now that we've discussed what grooming might look like we're going to run through a scenario. So we'd like you to consider the following behaviour and think about what it might mean and what the perceptions or the reality could be. So if you just look to number one so you notice that Tony a fellow coach who was a 28 year old man seems to be paying an excessive amount of attention to one of his athletes Monica who is a 14 year old girl. He often drives her home alone after training. He ignores other players in group sessions. You recently saw them alone at the local park doing a fitness session and other

players have seen them having lunch at a local cafe together. Yesterday he left his phone on the desk open with images on the screen showing training footage of Monica. Now that footage was still shots from a position behind Monica when she was serving and landing in the arabesque position. Now the worst case scenario here is that Tony is grooming Monica for later abuse. However it might also be something as simple as Tony being extremely passionate about coaching wanting to give Monica the best chance to succeed and not recognising the perceptions he's creating and the boundaries he's crossing. So three possible ways this scenario could unfold are firstly one and this is our preferred option somebody reporting their concerns to the integrity team so that we can make some inquiries and deliver a proportionate and independent response. In a recent similar matter we dealt with we made some initial inquiries which included speaking to the player's parents and no additional red flags were raised. We also spoke to the coach himself who explained his reasons for his actions including that the images on his phone were part of a serving technique analysis video that the player's parents had given him permission to work on. We gave him some professional guidance around his interactions, communication and training with child athletes to address the risks and the perceptions. A formal sanction will generally

only occur if the behaviour is particularly serious or if education has been tried and the behaviour continues. Another way that this particular scenario could play out is that a vigilant parent of another player sees these actions that we described of the coach and they start telling other parents how inappropriate the coach and player relationship is and how they hope that nothing is going on romantically between them. As you can imagine this room then spreads really quickly among the tennis community and Monica hears about the rumors from players also. So this creates anxiety and stress which negatively impacts on the player's performance and her results. So Monica then moves to another coach and the professional damage to Tony's reputation remains. In the worst case scenario, if nothing is said or reported, even if people around feel uncomfortable about Tony's behaviour, other people don't want to think the worst of a person, however Tony may actually be acting with inappropriate intentions. This intention may also form later due to professional boundaries being repeatedly crossed which potentially creates confusion in the player coach relationship. As a result, Monica is harmed and this harm could have been prevented by someone speaking up. It's really important to understand that not all people who offend against a child start out with the intention to harm or abuse a child. Often there are

times where professional boundaries have been repeatedly crossed and this may create confusion in a child in how they should be responding. It's fair to say that children often don't want to embarrass or criticise an adult. Victim survivors of abuse when telling of their experience have said things similar to, I didn't like what he was doing but I didn't know how to tell them to stop so I used to just laugh. And then so this type of response can then be interpreted as approval or enjoyment when the reality is the child is really uncomfortable and just doesn't know how to say so. Crossing professional boundaries even if it is done so completely innocently can put you in a position where it is difficult to defend yourself from allegations or poor perceptions. Community expectations in relation to ensuring child safe environments are changing and we need to be aware of this to protect our players, our professional reputation and businesses. We're all responsible as a collective group for maintaining the high standards of professionalism that we want to be held in. As coaches we need to maintain our awareness of the unique position of influence and trust that we hold. We need to keep front of mind the power imbalance in the coach and player relationship and the higher level of trust involved which in turn creates vulnerability in a junior athlete or child. And that is why it's up to other adults or coaches to call out actions that you may see

which are crossing professional boundaries or just don't feel right. Now we know this isn't easy or comfortable but it is the right thing to do if you see it happening. These actions taken then reduce the chance of things escalating and really do promote child safe environments. As coaches we ask for high standards from athletes and we need to hold ourselves to the same professional standards. If you need to take photographs or videos of junior athletes for training purposes make sure they and their parents or carers are aware of this. Ideally use the athletes or the parents device to take the footage. When it comes to things like demanding certain fitness metrics dietary requirements or training structures of your athlete if you can't articulate why you are setting these standards consider whether you should actually be doing that. We want to foster an athlete's understanding of what it takes for them to succeed. Wherever possible be aware of and avoid getting into situations with junior athletes where you may need to defend yourself or your reputation against difficult questions. For example avoid any unnecessary physical contact. Try not to be alone in private settings with junior players and don't message or be on social media with them about non-tennis specific things. Find ways to communicate with players in a safe and appropriate way. If you are communicating with players via social media group chats or similar it's best practice to include parents or guardians

in the communications. We really need to make a priority the need to protect your own professional reputation and business rather than always focusing completely on the athlete. We also recommend conducting some self-reflection and seek feedback from athletes parents and other coaches. Don't be afraid of honest feedback or having your methods questioned and if you hear a colleague say something like but I've always done it this way and there's never been an issue I think that's where we want to use that moment as an opportunity to change their mindset towards always looking for ways that we can improve what we do. If you must connect with athletes on social media remember your professional boundaries are important here as well. It's super creepy for an older man to be making comments about how hot a teenage girl looks not to mention completely unprofessional if he's a coach. Unfortunately we have seen these types of comments being made in the past. Think of how your online behavior will be perceived by others. None of this is saying that you can't train hard coach effectively or place high standards on an athlete. You can still challenge them support them and be someone they enjoy working with without putting yourself at risk and more importantly while still creating a child safe and friendly environment. For a player to achieve at their highest level they need to be 100 committed. It's up to us as coaches to create

environments where they feel comfortable to bring this commitment and enjoy the challenge of their journey to becoming the best player and person they can be. So if you're interested to learn more about any of the real-life situations that we've touched on in this presentation today here are some good starting points for that information. And if you need to contact the Tennis Australia integrity team for any reason you can email us at integrity at tennis.com.au or make an anonymous phone report to stop line on the number on your screen 1300 117233. Of course if anyone needs help immediately please always contact police in the first instance on triple zero. On behalf of Lou and I thank you very much for your time. We really do appreciate it and all the best with your coaching and your businesses. We hope that you enjoy the rest of the conference. Thank you. Thanks.
